post_copy:
Alaska is 570,641 square miles of land, about 552 times Rhode Island's 1,034.
NSF's new AI Infrastructure Hubs program caps both at one award.

Ten awards are anticipated for fifty states. Most get nothing.
NSF's own word for the problem is uneven. Alaska's ceiling was set before anyone read a proposal.

The rule counts states. Alaska counts once from Ketchikan to Utqiagvik, and no state has more land. Rhode Island counts once too.

The rule in NSF's own words, the $100 million headline against the solicitation's range, and fifty states drawn at true land area.

Full proposals are due November 4th. An institution can be named on only one proposal. Someone at an Alaska university or nonprofit has 82 days to sort out whose name that is.

Is 82 days enough for Alaska's institutions to line up behind one proposal?

#AlaskaResearch #ResearchComputing #NSFFunding

aftercare: Post Tuesday through Thursday, 8 to 11am Alaska time. That window is when program officers, university staff and legislative aides are actually at a desk, and this deck is written for exactly those three.
Paste the sources comment within about 60 seconds of posting, so the first comment under the post is the citation list rather than a stranger's reply.

Reply to every comment in the first 60 to 90 minutes. The readers most likely to know something the documents do not carry are the ones who will comment early, and a fast reply is what earns the second one.

The 82 day figure is correct for August 14, 2026 and nothing else. If posting slips, the tick count on slide 8 and both mentions in the caption go stale and have to be recounted to November 4, 2026 before this ships.

Check saves and comments at 48 hours. Slide 6 is built to be screenshotted, so a save-heavy result is the argument for more ranked reference plates and a comment-heavy one is the argument for more closing sufficiency questions.
editor_notes_for_email: post_copy is the caption room's winner byte for byte, hashtag line included, at 869 characters with a 77 character hook. The deck disagrees with NSF using only NSF's own sentences, which is why slide 3 sets the rule verbatim and slide 5 hands the whole frame to the agency's own word for the problem, uneven. One award per state is treated throughout as a defensible design choice rather than a scandal, and slide 7 exists to make NSF's case properly before the deck declines it. Nowhere does the deck claim Alaska has applied, been refused, or lacks a credible proposer, because no fetched document supports any of that. The copywriter caught and the run fixed one real accuracy error on slide 2, which had asserted that ten awards will be made against a solicitation that says anticipates; it now reads NSF anticipates ten awards per cycle. Worth a human eye, the 82 day count is only true for a post on August 14, 2026.
